job.style: a comparison of two related ideas

passage: The Indian economy is divided into three main sectors based on the nature of economic activity. The primary sector involves the extraction of natural resources, which includes not only farming but also activities like fishing, forestry, and mining. When these natural products are changed into other forms through manufacturing, we enter the secondary sector. The tertiary sector provides essential services that support the other two, such as transport, banking, and communication. To measure the health of these sectors, we calculate the Gross Domestic Product (GDP), which is the total value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year. It is important to note that intermediate goods are excluded to avoid double counting. Furthermore, the government implements various schemes to support workers. For instance, the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) provides a legal guarantee of one hundred days of wage employment in a year to those who are able to, and are in need of, work in rural areas. This scheme specifically targets rural households rather than urban populations. By understanding these sectors and policies, we can better evaluate how the economy grows and how the government works to ensure livelihood security for its citizens.

items.evidence: The primary sector involves the extraction of natural resources, which includes not only farming but also activities like fishing, forestry, and mining.
items.q: Ravi earns his living by catching fish in a river. Which sector does he work in?
options: Primary, as he takes natural resources
Secondary, as he uses a motor boat
Tertiary, as he sells his catch daily
None, as primary covers only farming
items.explain: Fishing takes natural resources directly, and the primary sector includes fishing, forestry and mining, not only farming.

wrong.why: thinks using a machine makes work secondary
focuses on selling instead of the main activity
thinks the primary sector is only farming

items.evidence: The tertiary sector provides essential services that support the other two, such as transport, banking, and communication.
items.q: A truck company carries cotton from farms to mills. Which sector is it in?
options: Tertiary, as it provides a support service
Secondary, as it runs heavy machines
Primary, as it carries farm products
Secondary, as it helps factories make goods
items.explain: Transport is a service that supports the other two sectors, so it belongs to the tertiary sector.

wrong.why: thinks using machines makes it secondary
judges by the goods carried, not the activity
mixes up helping manufacturing with doing manufacturing

items.evidence: To measure the health of these sectors, we calculate the Gross Domestic Product (GDP), which is the total value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year.
items.q: A country's banks and schools make no goods. Do their services count in its GDP?
options: Yes, GDP counts both goods and services
No, GDP counts only goods produced
No, services add nothing of real value
Yes, but only services sold to other countries
items.explain: GDP is the value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year.

wrong.why: thinks GDP is only the sum of goods
thinks the tertiary sector adds nothing to GDP
misses that GDP counts output within the country

items.evidence: It is important to note that intermediate goods are excluded to avoid double counting.
items.q: To find GDP, should wheat sold to a flour mill be added separately?
options: No, its value is already in the flour
Yes, every stage's value must be added
Yes, GDP is the sum of all goods
No, farm goods are never part of GDP
items.explain: Wheat is an intermediate good; its value is already in the flour, so adding it would count twice.

wrong.why: thinks intermediate goods are added at each stage
thinks GDP adds up every good produced
over-generalises the rule to all farm goods

items.evidence: This scheme specifically targets rural households rather than urban populations.
items.q: Ramesh lives in a big city and needs work. Can he get 100 days' work under MGNREGA?
options: No, the scheme is meant for village households
Yes, it gives work to everyone who needs it
No, he must first own some farm land
Yes, if he once worked in a factory
items.explain: MGNREGA targets rural households, not people living in cities, so Ramesh cannot use it.

wrong.why: thinks MGNREGA gives work to everyone, even in cities
thinks a job is given only to land owners
invents a work-experience condition not in the passage
